title: Shared For-Header Control Flow, Liveness, and Cleanup Semantics
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0493 | DEA-CANON-0494 | DEA-CANON-0495 | DEA-CANON-0496 | DEA-CANON-0499 | DEA-CANON-0500
architectural_question: Which statements may occur in for initialization/update clauses, which loop receives abrupt control, and how do those paths affect execution order, definite return, and cleanup?
chosen_decision: Keep ordinary abrupt simple statements in headers; allow declarations only in initialization; target an already-enclosing loop from header break/continue; preserve init/condition/body/update order; and compute definite flow only from paths guaranteed to execute while honoring with cleanup exit replacement.
alternatives: Restrict headers to a non-abrupt BasicStmt grammar | Treat header break/continue as targeting the loop whose header is executing | Infer definite return from body/update paths that may execute zero times
rationale: The adopted model preserves the existing expressive grammar while making target selection, sequencing, liveness, and deterministic cleanup explicit across compiler stages.
consequences: Parser, analyzer, backend, and cleanup lowering must share one control-flow model | Header updates run after body continue, but body/update returns do not prove function return | Invalid or impossible exits cannot corrupt later reachability analysis

title: L0 Release Identity, Integrity, and Immutable Publication
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0140 | DEA-CANON-0145 | DEA-CANON-0146 | DEA-CANON-0353 | DEA-CANON-0354 | DEA-CANON-0355 | DEA-CANON-0359 | DEA-CANON-0552 | DEA-CANON-0553 | DEA-CANON-0554
architectural_question: What identity, review gate, integrity manifest, and publication lifecycle define an official L0 release?
chosen_decision: Stable releases use public-repository-only l0-vX.Y.Z tags mapped one-to-one to checked-in notes, assemble complete drafts before publication, never mutate a published release, and publish a complete bare-name SHA-256 manifest; manual snapshots remain explicit prerelease/draft flows.
alternatives: Bare date-based vYYYY-MM-DD tags | Generate release bodies from Git history | Publish assets incrementally into a live release | Publish duplicate releases from the private monorepo | Sign every artifact in the initial release baseline
rationale: Release identity and publication side effects are public, difficult to reverse, and high-risk when inferred from workflow implementation alone.
consequences: Tag validation, curated notes, asset staging, checksum completeness, sole-target enforcement, and post-publication immutability remain mandatory release gates.

title: Compiler Diagnostic Collection, Parser Recovery, and Phase Barriers
architectural_question: How do compiler frontends accumulate errors, recover a partial parse, and decide whether later semantic/code-generation phases may run?
chosen_decision: Use diagnostic collectors as the authoritative channel, recover at declaration and current-block statement boundaries, preserve braces during synchronization, make an unmatched block close at EOF terminal for parser recovery, return partial parse state, and gate semantic/code generation—not parsing—after accumulated recoverable errors.
alternatives: Fail fast through public lexer/parser exceptions | Recover only between top-level declarations | Run semantic analysis on a partial AST containing syntax errors
rationale: A shared partial-result contract permits multiple useful diagnostics without letting malformed structure leak into semantic or backend phases.
consequences: Stage implementations may differ physically but must preserve logical recovery behavior | Parser APIs own partial results plus accumulated diagnostics | Recovery loops require explicit structural and EOF termination invariants

title: Intentional Cross-Level Divergence and Parity Exceptions
architectural_question: When may an unreleased downstream level intentionally advance ahead of the L0/Stage 1 oracle, and how is that divergence distinguished from a defect?
chosen_decision: An unreleased level may land a forward-only migration first, but every oracle mismatch must be explicit, narrowly scoped, and recorded as a parity skip until the upstream level catches up.
alternatives: Require lockstep language migrations across every level | Allow silent oracle divergence | Disable parity suites during forward migrations
rationale: Independent level evolution is useful, but explicit skips are required to preserve the oracle's ability to detect accidental drift.
consequences: Parity fixtures need named exceptions with retirement conditions; forward migrations must identify affected diagnostics and cannot normalize unrelated divergence.

title: Shared Integer Standard-Library Naming and Failure Contract
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0232 | DEA-CANON-0233 | DEA-CANON-0234 | DEA-CANON-0235 | DEA-CANON-0237 | DEA-CANON-0238 | DEA-CANON-0251 | DEA-CANON-0252 | DEA-CANON-0253 | DEA-CANON-0254
architectural_question: How do shared int and L1 wide-integer helper families encode type width, precondition errors, and representability failure in their public APIs?
chosen_decision: Keep shared int helpers unsuffixed; use _ui/_l/_ul for wide families; assert invalid caller preconditions; return plain values for total or contract-constrained operations and nullable values for domain/representability failure.
alternatives: Suffix shared int helpers with _i | Use overloads | Return nullable values for every arithmetic helper | Panic on all representability failures | Require uint callers to widen to ulong
rationale: Explicit width names avoid overload ambiguity while the result-type split distinguishes caller contract violations from mathematically valid but unrepresentable results.
consequences: L0/L1 shared APIs retain unsuffixed int names, L1 wide families follow fixed suffixes, and callers must handle null only for checked operations.

title: Top-Level Let Inference and Runtime-Initialization Boundaries
architectural_question: Which top-level let initializers may omit a type and which may require runtime module initialization across L0 and L1?
chosen_decision: L0's self-hosted semantic foundation limits unannotated top-level inference to primitive literals and constructor-style calls, while L1 permits arbitrary top-level runtime expressions and defers nonconstant initialization to module initialization.
alternatives: Require explicit types for every top-level binding | Permit unrestricted inference and runtime initialization at every level | Restrict all top-level initializers to compile-time constants
rationale: The levels intentionally expose different bootstrap capability while keeping initialization and type-inference boundaries explicit.
consequences: Cross-level ports cannot assume identical top-level initializer capability | L1 backend/lifecycle logic must schedule nonconstant initialization | L0 diagnostics must request annotations outside its narrow inference set

title: Amend ADR-0014: Platform-Specific Bootstrap Artifact Identity and Provenance
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0113 | DEA-CANON-0123 | DEA-CANON-0128 | DEA-CANON-0129 | DEA-CANON-0545 | DEA-CANON-0551
architectural_question: What constitutes a self-hosting fixed point when native artifacts contain toolchain- and platform-specific nondeterminism, and where may provenance enter?
chosen_decision: Retained C is always compared raw across compiler generations; native identity is normalized or waived by platform/toolchain, executable artifacts are not mutated merely for comparison, bootstrap compilers omit provenance, and release provenance enters through a generated source overlay.
alternatives: Require raw native byte identity on every toolchain | Skip all native identity checks | Strip or patch the actual executable artifacts | Inject provenance through wrapper plumbing or post-link patching
rationale: The rule preserves a meaningful compiler fixed point without confusing loader metadata or nondeterministic PE/TinyCC output with semantic compiler drift.
consequences: Linux, Windows, TinyCC, Intel Darwin, and arm64 Darwin use explicit comparison policies. | Comparison normalization may operate on copies but must not weaken raw retained-C identity. | Release-bearing provenance is kept outside raw bootstrap generations.

title: L0 Safe Standard-Stream Byte I/O Boundary
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0088 | DEA-CANON-0089 | DEA-CANON-0091 | DEA-CANON-0092 | DEA-CANON-0093 | DEA-CANON-0094 | DEA-CANON-0095 | DEA-CANON-0096
architectural_question: What buffer type, range discipline, failure channel, and raw-memory boundary govern safe standard-stream byte operations?
chosen_decision: Safe std.io uses fixed-capacity ByteArray subranges with assertion-checked bounds; read/write progress uses counts and null for I/O failure, EOF is zero, write-all treats zero progress as failure, and raw-pointer operations stay in the low-level memory module.
alternatives: Expose raw pointers directly from std.io | Use growable buffers or implicit whole-buffer operations | Represent EOF and I/O failure with one sentinel | Treat invalid ranges as nullable I/O failures
rationale: The split preserves a safe default API while keeping raw-memory escape hatches explicit and distinguishing program-contract errors from external I/O failure.
consequences: Callers pass explicit start/count ranges, zero-length operations remain valid, partial progress stays observable, and unsafe raw access is not accidentally re-exported through std.io.

title: L0 Stage 2 Arena-Backed AST and Parser Ownership Model
architectural_question: How should the self-hosted Stage 2 parser represent AST identity and transfer ownership of parsed modules and arenas?
chosen_decision: Use pointer-owned declarations/shared metadata with arena-backed expression, statement, and pattern nodes referenced by integer IDs; ParseResult owns the module and arenas until released as one aggregate.
alternatives: Individually heap-allocate every AST node | Use an entirely pointer-linked AST | Transfer individual arena ownership to downstream phases
rationale: The hybrid model gives stable compact IDs for dense syntax nodes while preserving pointer identity where declarations and shared metadata need it.
consequences: Downstream Stage 2 phases depend on arena lifetime through ParseResult | AST APIs must distinguish pointer-owned and ID-addressed node families | Large representation changes require coordinated parser/analyzer migration

title: L0 Stage 2 Driver and Host-Process Boundary
architectural_question: Which responsibilities belong to the Stage 2 build driver, and how may the self-hosted compiler invoke and interpret host compiler/linker processes?
chosen_decision: The l0c facade owns build orchestration and invokes host tools through std.system; runtime status values are normalized, while platform-specific command construction is confined to the driver/host boundary.
alternatives: Introduce a new general subprocess abstraction in the compiler | Expose raw C `system()` wait-status words | Use one POSIX shell command grammar on every host | Keep host-process orchestration in the public CLI module | Let each command mode parse and normalize its own inputs
rationale: The orchestration split and process-execution contract are one architectural boundary: together they keep host shell behavior out of compiler phases while preserving a portable self-hosted driver.
consequences: Command rendering is host-specific. | The runtime owns child-status normalization. | Stage 2 has no independent general subprocess surface. | CLI parity changes land at the l0c boundary | Host command construction and execution remain testable behind build_driver

title: L0 Supported Host, Toolchain, and Release Artifact Tiers
architectural_question: Which hosts and Windows toolchain environments are first-class L0 build/release targets, and what relocatability guarantees do their artifacts provide?
chosen_decision: Release binaries target Linux x86_64, macOS x86_64/arm64, and Windows x86_64; UCRT64 with MSYS2 Python is the automatic Windows tier, MINGW64/native Python are manual supported tiers, and Windows distribution builds statically link the GCC runtime unless explicitly overridden.
alternatives: Ship fewer binary targets | Use MINGW64 or MSVC as the automatic Windows baseline | Depend on libwinpthread/GCC runtime DLLs in the distribution | Treat manual Windows configurations as unsupported
rationale: A documented tier model aligns CI, support claims, and downloadable artifact portability.
consequences: Release workflows maintain a four-artifact platform matrix. | Windows CI and manual lanes intentionally differ. | Default Windows distributions avoid an undeclared runtime DLL dependency.

title: L0 Time Model, Public Values, and Runtime Boundary
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0046 | DEA-CANON-0047 | DEA-CANON-0048 | DEA-CANON-0049 | DEA-CANON-0050 | DEA-CANON-0051 | DEA-CANON-0052 | DEA-CANON-0053
architectural_question: What time domains and value/failure contracts does L0 expose, and which clock/calendar responsibilities belong to the runtime versus the language standard library?
chosen_decision: L0 exposes distinct WallTime, MonotonicTime, Duration, and DateTime values with optional failure and normalized nanoseconds; the runtime supplies wall/monotonic snapshots and local offset/DST facts, while language code performs UTC calendar conversion and monotonic time never falls back to wall time.
alternatives: Read seconds and nanoseconds through separate calls | Fall back from monotonic to wall-clock time | Delegate both UTC and local calendar conversion to libc | Implement host timezone rules in the language library | Use one generic timestamp type | Panic or return sentinel values on conversion failure | Permit denormalized nanosecond fields | Represent leap seconds
rationale: One ADR should keep public time semantics, failure behavior, normalization, and the host/runtime boundary coherent because changing any one of them constrains the others.
consequences: Clock availability is explicit in the API. | The runtime ABI returns a coherent two-field snapshot. | UTC conversion is portable integer arithmetic; local conversion remains host-dependent. | APIs cannot freely mix wall and monotonic values; callers handle null; DateTime second remains 0..59; runtime adapters normalize platform values.

title: L0 Toolchain Installation and Distribution Layout
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0105 | DEA-CANON-0106 | DEA-CANON-0107 | DEA-CANON-0116 | DEA-CANON-0135 | DEA-CANON-0137 | DEA-CANON-0138 | DEA-CANON-0139 | DEA-CANON-0143 | DEA-CANON-0144
architectural_question: What constitutes a runnable, relocatable L0 toolchain across repo-local, installed-prefix, and binary-distribution contexts?
chosen_decision: Keep repo-local stage selection explicit and checkout-relative, while installed and distributed Stage 2 toolchains are self-contained, relocatable, omit Stage 1, carry shared assets and version metadata, and use host-native launch/archive forms.
alternatives: Install Stage 1 alongside Stage 2 | Use one checkout-bound layout for installs and distributions | Give distributions a separate layout from installed prefixes | Require ambient L0_HOME configuration
rationale: One relocatable installed-prefix contract minimizes layout drift while preserving an explicit bootstrap/developer distinction.
consequences: Launchers and assets must resolve relative to the selected layout; distribution tests must cover POSIX and Windows forms; Stage 1 remains a build oracle rather than a shipped dependency.

title: L1 Case Value Comparability and Unreachable-Arm Policy
architectural_question: How do case arm values relate to equality compatibility, and what happens to a well-formed arm outside the scrutinee's value domain?
chosen_decision: Case uses equality comparability over the supported builtin families; an out-of-domain integer arm is valid but warned as always false, its body is still type-checked, and it does not become a viable runtime branch.
alternatives: Require exact arm-literal and scrutinee types | Reject out-of-domain integer arms as errors | Skip type checking bodies of statically impossible arms
rationale: Reusing equality compatibility keeps dispatch coherent with operators, while warning preserves useful diagnostics without hiding errors in unreachable source.
consequences: Case typing and equality conversion rules must evolve together | Reachability classification is separate from ordinary type checking | Out-of-domain arms need a stable warning and lowering policy

title: L1 Named-Call Syntax, Completeness, and Evaluation Order
architectural_question: Which call surfaces accept labels, may labels mix with positional arguments, and how do label mapping and side-effect order interact?
chosen_decision: Top-level functions and constructors accept label: expression arguments; a call is entirely positional or named; every label appears exactly once; labels map to declaration order while expressions evaluate left-to-right in written order.
alternatives: Allow positional arguments followed by named arguments | Evaluate named arguments in parameter/declaration order | Permit omitted labels through default arguments
rationale: The rule gives deterministic completeness and preserves visible side-effect order without introducing defaults or mixed-call ambiguity.
consequences: Backends must stabilize source-order evaluation before parameter reordering | Function-pointer calls and compiler intrinsics remain outside the named surface | Unknown, duplicate, and omitted labels are static errors

title: L1 Pointer Equality and Ordering Semantics
architectural_question: Do L1 pointer comparisons use reference identity, what compatibility is required, and is address ordering meaningful?
chosen_decision: Same-type non-null pointers compare by identity with == and !=; different pointer types require an explicit cast, and ordered pointer comparisons are rejected.
alternatives: Implicitly coerce every pointer type through void* for equality | Define ordering over host addresses | Reject all pointer comparison
rationale: Identity equality is useful and portable enough for same-type references, while cross-type coercion and address ordering would import host-C assumptions into L1.
consequences: Pointer equality remains nominally type-strict | Users must cast deliberately for heterogeneous identity checks | Sorting or relational comparison of addresses is not a language operation

title: L1 Real-Library Runtime and Host-Math Linkage Boundary
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0243 | DEA-CANON-0244 | DEA-CANON-0245 | DEA-CANON-0246 | DEA-CANON-0247 | DEA-CANON-0248
architectural_question: How does L1 expose floating-point library operations without overloads, compiler intrinsics, or unconditional host-math linkage?
chosen_decision: Expose `std.real` over `sys.real`, use explicit `_f`/`_d` APIs and public result structs, implement operations through a gated runtime helper header, and link the host math library only when those helpers are used.
alternatives: Name the module std.float | Add compiler intrinsics or backend special cases | Use overloads rather than explicit width suffixes | Link libm for every program using float or double
rationale: The boundary keeps the compiler generic, the pre-overload API explicit, and plain floating programs free of unnecessary host linkage.
consequences: Helper use is tracked separately from scalar type use. | Generated C conditionally includes l1_real.h. | Only real-library users receive the host math link dependency.

title: L1 Runtime Archive and Trace-Selection Boundary
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0339 | DEA-CANON-0340 | DEA-CANON-0341 | DEA-CANON-0343 | DEA-CANON-0344 | DEA-CANON-0345 | DEA-CANON-0346 | DEA-CANON-0347 | DEA-CANON-0348
architectural_question: What is the L1 runtime artifact boundary, how are trace variants selected, and how does that boundary coexist with TinyCC and L0?
chosen_decision: L1 uses declaration-only public headers backed by normal and traced archives selected by the driver; official archives use the platform object format, incompatible TinyCC uses parallel raw objects, traced wrappers preserve their public ABI while generated calls carry source locations directly, and L0 remains header-only at the 1.0 boundary.
alternatives: Keep L1's runtime header-only | Toggle tracing at runtime or in each user C translation unit | Maintain a compatibility l1_runtime.h shim | Require one archive format to serve incompatible TinyCC objects | Backport the archive split to L0
rationale: A real L1 library establishes the link model needed by separate compilation while retaining deterministic tracing and supported compiler-family behavior without destabilizing L0.
consequences: The driver, not user C preprocessor toggles, selects the runtime variant. | The public install surface excludes internal SipHash implementation headers. | TinyCC may link raw runtime objects while other toolchains consume archives. | L0 and L1 intentionally retain different runtime packaging models.

title: Documentation Publication Ownership and Cross-Repository Boundary
canonical_decision_ids: DEA-CANON-0072 | DEA-CANON-0149 | DEA-CANON-0150 | DEA-CANON-0152 | DEA-CANON-0153 | DEA-CANON-0154
architectural_question: Which repository owns documentation export, import, commit, deployment, and publication authorization?
chosen_decision: Dea owns canonical docs and export artifacts, validation never publishes, blog synchronization is opt-in and artifact-based, notification is optional, and each destination repository owns its own import, commit, and deployment workflow.
alternatives: Have Dea directly check out, commit, and push the destination repository | Make destination credentials mandatory for Dea documentation builds | Apply destination-specific normalization to canonical generated Markdown
rationale: Separating artifact production from destination publication reduces credential coupling and preserves independent repository governance.
consequences: Cross-repository writes require explicit authorization; missing destination configuration cannot break canonical docs production; the destination controls branch and deployment behavior.

title: Shared Editor Tooling, Level Identities, and Compiler Authority
architectural_question: How should one shared editor implementation represent distinct language levels without becoming a competing semantic authority?
chosen_decision: Maintain one shared editor package with distinct L0/L1 public identities; use an error-tolerant L1-superset Tree-sitter grammar for structure, defer LSP semantics, and keep the compiler authoritative.
alternatives: Separate editor repositories or packages per language level | Expose one undifferentiated Dea language identity | Treat Tree-sitter acceptance as normative language validity | Implement semantic validation independently in each editor
rationale: Shared syntax infrastructure avoids duplication while distinct identities and a compiler-authority boundary prevent silent level or semantic drift.
consequences: Editor parsers must tolerate incomplete code, level mappings remain separate, and future LSP work must derive semantics from compiler contracts rather than editor grammar acceptance.

title: Shared Standard-Library Naming and Compatibility Policy
architectural_question: How are shared public stdlib modules and specialized containers named, and what compatibility policy applies to pre-release renames?
chosen_decision: Use intent-revealing module names such as sys.memory and std.integer, normalize specialized types to type-before-container order, and make pre-release renames as hard source breaks without compatibility aliases or shim modules.
alternatives: Retain sys.unsafe and std.math | Keep container-first specialization names | Ship forwarding modules and type/function aliases | Allow a mixed-name transition period
rationale: A single canonical spelling prevents long-lived duplicate APIs and makes module/type intent visible before compatibility commitments harden.
consequences: Imports, qualified names, helper prefixes, docs, tests, and L1 mangled names migrate atomically; old spellings remain historical only.

title: L0 Filesystem Metadata and Recoverable File-Read ABI
architectural_question: Which filesystem metadata and file-read edge conditions cross the L0 runtime ABI?
chosen_decision: The runtime returns a stable file-info metadata record, and empty files, short reads, and end-of-file remain recoverable outcomes rather than fatal runtime failures.
alternatives: Use several independent metadata calls | Require full transfers or panic | Treat unsupported file kinds as compiler/runtime failures
rationale: A compact runtime boundary exposes ordinary host-I/O uncertainty to library code without converting expected environmental conditions into internal failures.
consequences: Metadata availability is represented explicitly. | Empty files, short reads, and end-of-file remain ordinary recoverable cases. | Host filesystem edge cases do not become compiler/runtime internal failures.

title: L0 Runtime Trace Source Provenance
architectural_question: How do ARC and memory runtime trace events preserve the originating Dea source location across generated C?
chosen_decision: Trace records carry a source location field captured by macro-wrapped runtime entry points through `__FILE__` and `__LINE__`, with generated-C `#line` directives mapping those values back to Dea.
alternatives: Record only generated-C locations | Pass explicit source-location arguments at every L0 runtime call | Omit source provenance from runtime traces
rationale: Runtime traces are useful for ownership archaeology only when events can be attributed to the originating Dea operation.
consequences: Trace ABI and tooling preserve a `loc` field. | Generated-C line directives and runtime entry macros form one provenance contract.

title: L0 Stage 2 Semantic Result and Pass-Ordering Architecture
architectural_question: What owns Stage 2 semantic state, and in what order are module environments, declarations, and imports established?
chosen_decision: One AnalysisResult owns driver state, environments, signatures, local scopes, and one authoritative diagnostic collector; name resolution creates module environments, collects local declarations, and opens imports while diagnostics accumulate throughout analysis.
alternatives: Return independent pass-owned tables with unrelated lifetimes | Resolve imports before collecting every module's local declarations | Mutate parser-owned state as the semantic result
rationale: A single ownership boundary and explicit pass order make cross-module resolution deterministic and keep self-hosted cleanup tractable.
consequences: Semantic consumers receive one lifetime-bearing aggregate | Import opening can rely on complete local declaration environments | Pass reordering becomes an architectural change rather than a local refactor
